title: Time-domain astronomy at Cerro Tololo
caption: The Milky Way above Las Cumbres Observatory telescopes, Cerro Tololo, Chile
celestial: Photograph taken at Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory, Chile
credit: CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/P. Horálek (Institute of Physics in Opava), M. Kosari

recognition.text: NOIRLab Image of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: The Milky Way stretches across the sky above Cerro Tololo Inter-American Observatory in Chile in this wide panorama. Besides its biggest and best-known telescopes, Cerro Tololo hosts around 40 telescopes run by 11 tenant observatories and research projects.

This view features several of them. On the left are three 1-meter telescopes of the Las Cumbres Observatory, with the “igloo” in the center housing one of its spectrographs, and on the right is the Planetary Defense 1.3-meter Telescope.

Las Cumbres runs a network of telescopes spread around the globe, so it can keep watch on an object around the clock as Earth turns. That is essential for time-domain astronomy, the study of things in the sky that change over seconds, days or weeks rather than millions of years, such as supernovae and gamma-ray bursts.

understand.summary: A ground-based landscape photograph credited to CTIO/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA/P. Horálek (Institute of Physics in Opava), M. Kosari. The source does not publish camera, exposure or color-processing details.
understand.eye: A camera can gather light for longer than the eye, so the Milky Way looks brighter and more detailed here than it would to someone standing on site.
